clue.text: The frets she gets in — producing floods!

indicators.note: the word she gets into the middle of frets, so one piece is placed inside the other

explanation.surface: Someone frets about a deluge she lets in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets in' signals the container. A freshet is a river's spring flood from melting snow or heavy rain; the surface's fretting woman is a distraction.
explanation.definitionFit: Freshets are sudden rises of a river after rain or thaw, a kind of flood.

clue.text: Why Rabbie took a right waught.

definitions.text: Why Rabbie took a right waught.

parts.words: Why Rabbie took a right waught.
parts.note: Rabbie is Robert Burns; his song of old times past has the line about taking 'a right gude-willie waught' (a hearty drink), and the reason he gives is its refrain

explanation.surface: A question about why the Scottish poet Burns took a big swig.
explanation.walkthrough: Burns's New Year song says 'we'll tak a right gude-willie waught, for auld lang syne': a waught is a Scots word for a deep draught of drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's refrain gives the reason for the drink: in remembrance of old times long past.

clue.text: Just lugged

parts.note: lugs is a homely word for ears, so being merely lugged means simply having ears, not having been hauled along

explanation.definitionFit: Lugs are ears, so something possessing lugs has ears, nothing more.

clue.text: That cheat of a milliner, getting out like this?

definitions.meaning: a hatmaker's trick or swindle, read literally as a trick with a hat
in cricket, a bowler getting three batsmen out with consecutive balls

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a hat-trick is three wickets from three successive deliveries; the bowler was traditionally rewarded with a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A milliner makes hats, so his deceit is a trick involving hats; a cricketer's three quick dismissals carry the same name.

clue.text: Probably a sound idea, whichever way you look at it.

indicators.text: whichever way you look at it
indicators.note: the word reads identically from left to right and right to left, so it looks the same from either direction

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A sensible notion is sound however you view it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'whichever way you look at it' says the answer is the same read backwards, so the whole wordplay is the answer's own shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A principle firmly held is a belief or doctrine, a sound idea one holds.

clue.text: Having a hunch and so upset.

definitions.meaning: with a hunched or rounded back, literally bearing a hump
having the hump is British slang for being sulky or annoyed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hunch' tempts as an intuition, but it means a hump on the back. 'To have the hump' is British slang for being in a sulk.
explanation.definitionFit: A hunched back is a humped back, and someone in a bad mood is said to have the hump.

clue.text: Away with punctuation!

parts.note: stops are punctuation marks, so doing away with them reads as taking the stops away; really the word means removing a stopper or blockage

explanation.definitionFit: Full stops are punctuation, so removing a stop, as from a bottle or a pipe, is clearing it.

clue.text: A nice point, showing some polish.

definitions.text: A nice point, showing some polish.

parts.words: A nice point, showing some polish.
parts.note: nice here means fine or precise, so a nice point is a fine detail of correct behaviour, the sort of thing a polished, refined person observes

explanation.definitionFit: A fine detail of etiquette or conduct, observed scrupulously by a well-mannered person.

clue.text: Suitable progress of a high jumper?.:

definitions.meaning: the phrase is used in 'suits me ...', meaning entirely fitting
after clearing the bar, an athlete's path is all the way back to earth

explanation.walkthrough: The British idiom 'it suits me down to the ground' means it suits completely.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means thoroughly fitting, and a jumper's descent goes literally all the way to earth.

clue.text: Ladies' small cloak lent mate for change.

indicators.note: the letters of the words lent mate are swapped about for a change, signalling an anagram

explanation.surface: Someone lends a friend a lady's cape to change into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for change' rearranges the letters of LENT MATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A short cape or mantle once worn by women is a diminutive of mantle.

clue.text: Upon which one's strength may depend.

definitions.text: Upon which one's strength may depend.

parts.words: Upon which one's strength may depend.
parts.note: a tendon is what muscle power relies on, and figuratively the word means the mainstay of strength

explanation.definitionFit: A tendon joining muscle to bone, and figuratively the source of power or vigour.

clue.text: As this is apart, it's below!

indicators.note: the words say the answer is what joins As to make apart, so As is removed from the synonym

parts.note: apart means asunder, torn in pieces
taken as written

explanation.surface: A puzzling remark that something set apart lies beneath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As this is apart' means As plus the answer gives ASUNDER (apart), so 'this is' takes AS away from ASUNDER.
explanation.definitionFit: Beneath and below are synonyms for lower than something.

clue.text: One kind of quid pro quo.

definitions.text: One kind of quid pro quo.

parts.words: One kind of quid pro quo.
parts.note: a quid pro quo is something given in return; one form is retaliation, blow for blow

explanation.definitionFit: Retaliation in kind, returning like for like, is a form of exchange of something for something.

clue.text: Likely to come off without much

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Likely to come off without much (10)', cut short after 'much': whatever completes the clue is missing; not found by search.
annotationWithheld.clue: Likely to come off without much

clue.text: Hardly the type you would expect to get elevated?

definitions.text: Hardly the type you would expect to get elevated?

parts.words: Hardly the type you would expect to get elevated?
parts.note: elevated is old slang for tipsy, so the clue describes a moderate person unlikely to get drunk

explanation.walkthrough: 'Elevated' looks like raised up or promoted, but it is slang for slightly drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A moderate person, abstemious with drink, is unlikely to become tipsy.

clue.text: Scholarly, yes, but not a gentleman to start this.

clue.text: Red grouse, unconfined Moscow.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Red grouse, unconfined Moscow.': no parse of 'unconfined Moscow' gives the wordplay; probably garbled in OCR, and not found by search.

clue.text: First class copy for one's designs.

parts.note: A1 means first class, here printed with letter I for the figure 1
MS is a manuscript, a written copy

explanation.surface: A top-quality copy of someone's plans.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 (first class) is printed in the grid with I for the figure 1.
explanation.definitionFit: Designs in the sense of intentions or purposes are goals one is trying for.

clue.text: Gee! All but a star expert epicurean!

parts.note: the letter G is spelt gee

indicators.note: all but means everything except the last letter of the word for a star expert

parts.note: an astronomer is an expert on stars

explanation.surface: An exclamation of delight at a near-star gourmet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All but' is a trimmed synonym: the star expert loses only his final letter. 'Gee!' looks like an exclamation but is the spelt-out letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An epicurean is a connoisseur of good food, a gourmet.

clue.text: Pedal variety of spinet.

definitions.note: pedal is an adjective meaning of the foot; the definition points to a part of the foot

indicators.note: a variety of the word spinet is a different arrangement of its letters

explanation.surface: A kind of small harpsichord worked by the feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety of' rearranges SPINET. 'Pedal' suggests a keyboard's pedal, but it means relating to the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: The arched middle of the foot is a foot part, so it is pedal in the anatomical sense.

clue.text: New condition — of a mug perhaps.

definitions.meaning: the state of being new or fresh, unripe
mug is British slang for a gullible fool, whose state is naivety

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mug' means a dupe in British slang, not a cup.
explanation.definitionFit: Freshness or newness, and also the inexperience or gullibility of a naive person.

clue.text: Indicative, this, of definite taste.

parts.note: the word describes something with a distinct flavour, rather than someone with discerning taste

explanation.definitionFit: Having a pronounced flavour, savoury and palatable, the opposite of insipid.

clue.text: Jockey's secondary proposition.

definitions.meaning: a jockey is someone on horseback
an addition to a document or a corollary in mathematics

explanation.walkthrough: A rider is also a clause added to a bill or a supplementary problem following a theorem.
explanation.definitionFit: A horseman, and also an added clause or corollary attached to a main statement.

clue.text: Station where they drank heavily on the way up?

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means the word is read from the bottom upward

parts.note: to tope is to drink heavily

explanation.surface: A pub-crawl stop where people drank hard on their journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the way up' turns TOPED to read the other way, as the entry runs down the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A bus or railway station is also called a terminus or depot in older usage.

clue.text: Yet on the greens at Rye a stymie may produce ferment!

indicators.note: the run of words Rye a stymie produces the answer from within its letters

explanation.surface: On a golf course at Rye, a stymie can stir things up.
explanation.walkthrough: Rye is a golf links in Sussex; a stymie was an old golf rule where a ball blocks another's path to the hole.
explanation.definitionFit: A leavening agent that causes fermentation.

clue.text: Sort of remark to show I'm quick and superior.'

parts.note: taken as written without the apostrophe
quick means prompt
U stands for upper class, a superior social rank

explanation.surface: A remark made to show off one's ready wit and class.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the old British label for upper-class usage.
explanation.definitionFit: An off-the-cuff remark is unrehearsed and spontaneous.

clue.text: Not called upon to serve.

parts.note: excused from duty such as military service or jury service

explanation.definitionFit: Free from an obligation, excused from duty or liability.
